claims.text: A single query of the authorized metrics returned one result: metric http_errors_rate with value 0.042, on target_id checkout-prod, status ok, result_count 1, returned_count 1, truncated false, omitted_rows 0.

The delivered metric point covers the fixed window start 2026-09-14T00:00:00+00:00 to end 2026-09-14T01:00:00+00:00, with data_as_of 2026-09-14T00:00:00+00:00 and observed_at 2026-09-16T14:45:33.022230+00:00 (freshness_seconds 225933.02223), so the value is roughly two and a half days older than the retrieval time.

No comparable baseline or prior-interval value for http_errors_rate was delivered, so the 0.042 value cannot be judged high or low relative to normal behavior; the premise that errors are 'elevated' is unsupported by the delivered evidence.

If HTTP errors are in fact elevated on the checkout path, the delivered aggregate is too coarse to localize the cause: it carries no service, route, status-code or endpoint labels, so any attribution would require additional labelled series that were not delivered.
Rejected: that the delivered evidence establishes a rising error trend on checkout. A single aggregate point in one window cannot demonstrate a trend, and no earlier comparable value was supplied.

Before acting on the 'elevated HTTP errors' report, have a human pull a comparable baseline interval for the same metric and target, plus per-service and per-status-code breakdowns and request volume, to determine whether 0.042 is anomalous.
